name: Design Directive
evidence_rating: ex-ante only, backed by one pre-reform causal price study; transposition due December 2027
summary: The Commission forecast that opening the market for visible car spare parts such as bumpers and lights would save consumers EUR 340-544 million a year once a 10-year transition ends. A pre-reform study comparing countries found design protection makes these parts about 5-8% more expensive, supporting the forecast, but the Directive has not yet been transposed and no savings have been measured.

indicators.objective: The proposal's financial statement contains no indicators section; the memorandum says the Commission will monitor the spare-parts market to see whether the EU-wide repair clause yields the predicted savings, and refers to indicators in Section 9 of the impact assessment
Open the spare-parts aftermarket to competition
indicators.indicator: Consumer savings of EUR 340-544m a year once the 10-year transition for existing designs ends; benefits rising EUR 4-13m a year during the transition
indicators.evidence: Not measured; transposition deadline December 2027. Ex-ante causal evidence (Herz & Mejer) finds design protection raises spare-part prices by about 5-8%.

indicators.indicator: Annual savings of EUR 6m from lower EU design fees and EUR 1.6m from simpler procedures
indicators.evidence: Not evaluated (fee changes apply via the parallel EU Design Regulation 2024/2822).

indicators.objective: Align national design laws with the EU system
indicators.indicator: Lower cost and more predictability for firms protecting designs across Member States

literature.citation: European Commission (2022), Impact Assessment accompanying the proposals to amend the Community Design Regulation and recast the Design Directive (executive summary SWD(2022) 369), SWD(2022) 368
literature.title: Impact Assessment accompanying the proposals to amend the Community Design Regulation and recast the Design Directive (executive summary SWD(2022) 369)
literature.outcomes: spare-part prices; consumer savings; registration costs
literature.headline: Liberalising must-match spare parts (option 1.2) would save consumers EUR 340-544m a year after a 10-year transition, matched by lost income for carmakers; lower fees save EUR 6m a year and simpler procedures EUR 1.6m
literature.summary_plain: The Commission expected that opening the market for visible car spare parts would save consumers EUR 340-544 million a year once fully in effect.

literature.citation: Herz & Mejer (2020), The effect of design protection on price and price dispersion: Evidence from automotive spare parts, MPRA Paper 104137
literature.title: The effect of design protection on price and price dispersion: Evidence from automotive spare parts
literature.method: difference-in-differences (cross-country variation in repair-clause coverage, detailed spare-part price data)
literature.direction: negative effect of design protection on consumers (supports reform)
literature.headline: Design protection raises spare-part prices by about 5-8%, with large differences across carmakers; lack of harmonisation plus pricing-to-market explains part of large cross-country price gaps for identical parts
literature.summary_plain: Comparing countries with and without a repair clause, the study finds design protection makes visible car spare parts about 5-8% more expensive - the kind of saving the Directive aims to unlock.
literature.quality: causal (DiD); pre-reform evidence, not an evaluation of the Directive
literature.interested_party: Co-author Mejer is European Commission staff (ec.europa.eu affiliation); the study fed the Commission's analysis

literature.citation: European Commission (2020), Evaluation of EU legislation on design protection, SWD(2020) 264
literature.title: Evaluation of EU legislation on design protection
literature.headline: Design protection system works well overall but has shortcomings: outdated procedures and fees, divergent national rules, and an unharmonised spare-parts aftermarket
literature.summary_plain: The Commission's 2020 review found EU design law worked well overall but was outdated and left the car spare-parts market split between countries.
